Autodesk Stock Is Falling. Investors Aren’t Sold on Its $3.6 Billion Deal.

By Nate Wolf

Updated May 29, 2026, 3:52 pm EDT / Original May 29, 2026, 8:16 am EDT

Autodesk posted strong quarterly earnings after the closing bell Thursday but a $3.6 billion deal to acquire software company MaintainX and expand into a new market spooked investors.

Shares of the design and engineering software company fell 3.8% to $231.69 on Friday, recovering from much deeper losses earlier in the session. It had fallen 19% this year as of Thursday’s close of trading.

Autodesk reported adjusted earnings of $2.99 a share on revenue of $1.93 billion in its fiscal first quarter. The results surpassed analysts’ expectations for earnings of $2.84 a share and $1.89 billion in revenue. The company also lifted its fiscal-year guidance for both metrics.

But earnings were overshadowed by Autodesk’s agreement to purchase MaintainX, a maintenance and operations software platform, for $3.6 billion in cash. The deal will expand Autodesk’s operations footprint with customers, which include engineers and builders, and feed more data into its artificial-intelligence models.

“We were really looking at this several years out in terms of all the strategic benefits both on AI as well as as a stand-alone operations business,” Janesh Moorjani, Autodesk’s chief financial officer told Barron’s in between meetings with investors.

Moorjani compared the acquisition with Autodesk’s $875 million purchase of PlanGrid in 2018, which kick-started its construction software business. MaintainX can be that same “cornerstone acquisition” for operations, he said.

Software companies are walking a tightrope in 2026 amid fears that AI tools will disrupt their businesses. In this case, the price tag and the fit between Autodesk and MaintainX were enough to send shares spiraling.

MaintainX expects to reach $135 million in annualized recurring revenue this year with annual growth above 50%. But the $3.6 billion figure is roughly 18 times expected 2027 revenue, BTIG analyst Nick Altmann estimated. That valuation represents a premium to software peers at a time when multiples have compressed.

Still, Altmann likes the purchase, arguing that MaintainX not only expands Autodesk’s presence in its customers’ workflow but also adds a rich data set useful for virtual modeling. BTIG maintained a Buy rating and a $300 target on Autodesk shares.

Oppenheimer analyst Ken Wong was also optimistic about the MaintainX deal, seeing operations as a “natural extension” of Autodesk’s role in the design and building process. Investors didn’t view things the same way.

“In addition to the price tag, investors are wary of potential organic growth moderation and execution risks as go-to-market synergies aren’t apparent,” Wong wrote in a note Friday. Nevertheless, the firm reiterated an Outperform rating and a $325 price target on the stock.

MaintainX isn’t profitable, UBS analyst Taylor McGinnis pointed out. Autodesk has its sights set on a 41% operating margin by fiscal 2029 and believes it can absorb MaintainX and still hit that target.

“We wonder if there’s less upside potential than before,” McGinnis said, maintaining a Buy rating and a $290 price target.

Autodesk remains one of the more popular software names on Wall Street. Of the 36 firms tracked by FactSet, 92% have the equivalent of a Buy rating on Autodesk shares. At least 10 analysts, however, lowered their price targets in the wake of the MaintainX deal.
